citation.title: Investigating Mind Perception in HRI through Real-Time Implicit and Explicit Measurements
citation.venue: Companion of the 2024 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, 139–141; research progress report

reading.source_scope_note: A three-page progress/methodology report with N = 160 collected but no analyzed outcome effects. Live human and Pepper action stimuli are paired with an implicit association task, explicit ratings and interviews. This is a methodological citation, not evidence of an age/generation effect, improved validity or implicit–explicit agreement.
access_limits: No outcome estimates, uncertainty intervals, analysis results, interview findings or power analysis are supplied.
The separate RW-IAT methods report, stimulus norming studies, dissertation and raw data were not independently read or reproduced.
Original IAT validation, questionnaire and cited psychology papers are not independently reviewed merely because their names appear in the bibliography.

study.status: The abstract and progress section explicitly state that 160 in-person observations were collected and analysis is future work. Do not transform research questions, expected contributions or previous-study claims into new results.
study.participants: Four age bands with 40 participants each: 18–28, 33–43, 48–58 and 63–73. The gaps exclude intervening ages; diversity and equal quotas do not establish population representativeness. Age, cohort, historical technology exposure and current familiarity are not separated by a cross-sectional grouping alone.
study.perceiver_measures: Seven pre-exposure individual-difference scales are cited: eyes-based mentalizing, body consciousness, negative robot attitudes, loneliness, action identification, positive/negative affect and anthropomorphism. The report does not supply their exact implementation, reliability, analyzed coefficients or causal effects.
study.stimuli: A live human actor and a Pepper humanoid perform matching action categories. Communicative examples include peek-a-boo, saluting, throwing a kiss and waving; noncommunicative examples include shooting an arrow, jogging, drinking and driving. Matching categories does not prove matched kinematics, appearance, duration, feasibility or perceptual salience.
study.setup: A switchable OLED screen is transparent during action presentation and opaque during evaluation. The report presents this as reducing modality changes and improving measurement; no comparison in this paper demonstrates an accuracy, reliability or ecological-validity gain.
study.implicit_task: The real-world IAT pairs human/robot action stimuli with high/low agency or experience categories and records responses, response times and mouse trajectories. Task associations and hesitation are not unique indicators of unconscious belief, prejudice, deception, actual mental capacity or a particular neural process.
study.explicit_task: A separate six-block task asks 1–7 ratings of agent/action capacities through 12 sentences, including hunger. After training, the fixed sequence is RW-IAT then explicit task then interview. This ordering can influence later ratings/interviews; implicit–explicit agreement is a question, not a reported finding.
study.related_validation: The report cites two prior online action-norming studies with 40 actions and 438 participations, and a concept-stimulus study with N = 274. These are separate referenced data, not new samples fully analyzed here or verified additional unique people. No independent validation coefficients are supplied in this short report.
study.analysis_limits: No scoring formula, IAT reliability, exclusions, missingness handling, order counterbalancing, prespecified model, multiplicity strategy or effect-size precision is reported. Their omission in a short progress paper is not proof that the research team never used them; the separate methods/data would be needed.
study.generalization: A controlled co-located observation task is closer to live action than static stimuli but is not natural conversation, autonomous field deployment, long-term relationship behavior or a validated clinical/individual diagnosis.

summary: Add no new entries. Enrich existing agency/experience attribution and anthropomorphism with a clearly marked progress-methods citation; keep the IAT versus social-bias distinction as a non-counting boundary. Correct a mixed Zhao version/year reference and the IDAQ paper identity. No results, generation effect, new trait definition or evidence of actual AI mentality is inferred.

evidence.quote: we will conduct a thorough analysis

findings.evidence_scope: A progress report describes comparing high/low agency associations and explicit 1–7 capability ratings for live human/Pepper actions. N = 160 has been collected, but analysis remains future work; this is a method citation, not an observed agency effect or independent replication.
findings.boundary: High/low task associations, explicit perceived capability, actual performance, causal control and moral agency differ. A matching action label does not isolate all agent-appearance/movement differences; no age or agent contrast has been demonstrated here.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: This progress/methods paper studies an existing construct and reports no new analyzed effect. Add the method and access limits rather than another behavior label.
findings.evidence_scope: The report proposes experience-related IAT pairings and direct ratings such as whether a robot can feel hunger, alongside live stimuli. No implicit–explicit agreement, experience-rating contrast or mechanism estimate is reported.
findings.boundary: Perceived experience is not actual sentience. A relative association task is not an absolute belief test, and a fixed implicit-before-explicit sequence may affect the comparison. No spontaneous robot feeling or neurological measure is supplied.

evidence.quote: 160 participants, evenly distributed across four age groups

findings.evidence_scope: The report considers observer scales, age bands, agent type and communicative action as determinants of mind attribution, and uses baseline questionnaires plus live tasks. Its sample diversity, equal quotas and real-time setup are methodological features rather than analyzed determinant effects.
findings.boundary: No causal personality or generation effect follows from planned correlations. Equal age quotas do not ensure representativeness; implicit ratings, explicit ratings, humanlike appearance and later behavior require separate evidence.

findings.definition: Producing outputs systematically skewed along social lines (gender, race, age, disability) from stereotyped associations absorbed in training, without intending to.
findings.novelty_rationale: This progress/methods paper studies an existing construct and reports no new analyzed effect. Add the method and access limits rather than another behavior label.

evidence.quote: binary structure of the implicit association task

findings.evidence_scope: The source uses an implicit association task for relative mind-capacity associations, not a study of discriminatory social outputs. The named method does not by itself establish bias in the ontology’s failure-mode sense.
findings.boundary: An implicit measure, a stereotyped association, socially harmful output and an unconscious human attitude are distinct. No analyzed result or individual diagnostic validity is established here; this boundary note does not fill a supporting-paper gap.

source_identity_checks.finding: Crossref verifies publication 11 March 2024, pages 139–141, DOI 10.1145/3610978.3638366. Separate author-listing references to another RW-IAT companion item are not replacements for this paper’s pagination.

The supplied text confirms completed data collection, unlike an entirely unstarted protocol, but still reports analysis/result discussion as future steps. No empirical outcome effect can be credited from this file.

methodological_limits: No analyzed effect, precision, reliability or causal mechanism supplied. Planned/expected advantages and prior-paper results cannot be presented as this paper’s findings.
Cross-sectional age bands confound age/cohort/exposure; quotas and background diversity do not establish representative sampling.
Live action categories do not control appearance, biological motion, expressivity and motor capability. Fixed task order may introduce carry-over.
Implicit association, mouse movement and verbal ratings measure different outcomes and are not unique markers of unconscious mind attribution or harmful bias.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Keijsers leaves implicit-mind attribution unresolved because it is not measured directly. This report proposes an explicit implicit/explicit measurement comparison, but supplies no analyzed result resolving that earlier limitation.
The embodied/disembodied distinction motivates richer stimuli, but live presentation does not by itself validate a universal claim about mind attribution or superiority over every other method.
Observer mind measures remain one-step outcomes. No later human–human transfer, schema mechanism or clinical benefit is tested in this progress report.
